notes.meaning: Micah cries out in sorrow. He feels like someone who goes looking for fruit after the harvest is over and finds nothing good left: no grapes, no sweet early fig. The picture means that good, godly people have become very hard to find. He longs to see the kind of real faith that people had in earlier days.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars disagree about who is speaking in verses 1-6. Some say it is the prophet himself, some say it is Zion (Jerusalem), and some say it is the faithful people of Israel.

notes.meaning: The "godly man" is someone who is both devoted to God and kind and faithful to others. Such people seem to have vanished. Instead, people treat each other like animals to be hunted. They lie in wait and set traps for their own neighbors, ready to ruin anyone's life or living to get ahead.

People are skilled at doing wrong with both hands. The leader asks for a bribe, the judge sells his verdict, and the rich and powerful man openly says what evil he wants. Then all three twist their plans together like strands of a rope, so that justice gets lost. Things are very bad when the people meant to protect what is right are the ones doing wrong.

Even the best of them is like a thorn bush. Anyone who gets close gets scratched and hurt. So the day the prophets warned about is coming. Prophets were God's "watchmen," like guards on a wall. This is the day of God's "visitation," when He comes to judge. On that day everything they hid will come out, and they will be thrown into confusion.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The NET Bible reads the line differently, as "the day you try to avoid by posting watchmen."

notes.meaning: Trust has broken down so badly that no one can be relied on. Not a neighbor, not a close friend or adviser, not even a man's own wife. A man must watch what he says even to the person closest to him, because she might betray him. It is a sad time when wise people must keep quiet even at home.

Even families fall apart. Children despise their parents, and a household turns against itself. Henry calls this a sign that a whole society has gone bad. Jesus later used this verse to describe how families would split over Him (Matthew 10:35-36).

Here the mood turns. When no one on earth can be trusted, Micah turns to God. He will watch for the LORD and wait patiently for Him, the God who saves. He is sure that God will hear his prayer. Feeling let down by people can push us to trust the One who never fails.

Now God's people speak, pictured as a woman, to their enemy, who is also pictured as a woman. "Don't gloat over me." God's people may fall, but they will rise again. Even while they sit in the darkness of trouble, the LORD Himself is their light. Their hope rests on God, not on how things look right now.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some critics think verses 8 and following were added by a later editor after the exile, though others reject this.

notes.meaning: God's people admit that they sinned and deserve God's anger. So they will bear it patiently instead of complaining. But they also trust that God will take up their case against the enemies who wronged them. In the end He will bring them out into the light. They will see His "righteousness," which here means God keeping His promises to them.

The enemy mocked God's people by asking, "Where is the LORD your God?" That enemy will see God rescue His people and will be covered with shame. She who trampled others will be trampled like mud in the street. This is not about enjoying revenge. It is joy at seeing God show that He is just.

A day is coming when Jerusalem's ruined walls will be built again. The harsh rule that held God's people down will be taken away. People will come streaming to her from far-off lands, from Assyria to Egypt and from sea to sea. Many saw this first in the return from exile in Babylon, and saw it point ahead to God gathering people from every nation.

differ.view: The promise reaches from the return from exile on to the church that Christ gathers from all nations.
These promises point to a future time when God will restore Israel as a nation.

notes.meaning: Before that bright day comes, the land must lie empty and ruined. This is the result of the people's own sinful deeds. The good promises should not make anyone forget that God takes sin seriously, even among His own people.

Micah prays for the people, asking God to care for them like a shepherd with his staff. They are His own flock, scattered and alone like sheep in a forest. He asks God to bring them back to graze in rich pastures like Bashan and Gilead, as in the old days. Since God led the prophet to pray this, the prayer is also a promise. Many Christians also read it as a prayer to Christ, the great Shepherd of His church.

God answers the prayer, and He promises even more than was asked. He will do wonders again, like the miracles He did when He brought Israel out of Egypt. What God did before shows what He can and will do again.

The nations that looked down on God's people will see these wonders and feel ashamed. All their strength will turn out to be useless. They will cover their mouths in stunned silence. They will be brought as low as the snake in Genesis that eats dust. Like creatures creeping from their holes, they will come out of their hiding places trembling, and they will fear the LORD.

Micah bursts into praise: no one is like our God! He forgives sin, lifting it off and carrying it away, and He passes over the wrongs of the "remnant," the faithful few He has kept for Himself. He does not stay angry forever. The reason is found in God Himself: He loves to show steady, loyal love and mercy.

differ.view: The "remnant" who receive this pardon are the people God has chosen by His grace.
God's mercy is offered widely, and He is ready to save any sinner who turns back to Him.

notes.meaning: God will once more be kind to His people. He will "tread down" their sins like a defeated enemy. When He forgives, He also breaks sin's power over us. He throws all their sins into the deep sea, the way He drowned Pharaoh's army. He does not throw them near the shore, where they might wash back up. When God forgives, He forgives completely and does not bring those sins up again.

The book ends with confidence in God's covenant, His binding promise to His people. Long ago He promised Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and He even sealed it with an oath. Now He will keep faith with them and show them His loving devotion. Zechariah, John the Baptist's father, saw this promise fulfilled when Christ came (Luke 1:72-73).
